video_title: America’s AI Boom Is Squeezing Main Street | Weekly Roundup
gist: Aiden Gerb (PGM Global/National Bank of Canada) argues the US 10-year yield surge reflects a higher priced Fed terminal rate driven by ~6.6% nominal GDP, not inflation or fiscal fears, while growth is dangerously narrow and AI-capex dependent and housing/Main Street are crushed; hosts and guest see policymakers debasing, engineering captive Treasury demand, and supporting stocks, while Europe (ECB hiking into stagflation, rising German bankruptcies) loses the export war to Japan.

themes.theme: Treasury yield drivers: Fed terminal-rate repricing

insights.claim: Aiden Gerb argues the surge in the US 10-year Treasury yield is not driven by inflation expectations (stuck near 2.4% for about six years) or term premia, both of which have barely moved.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Fiscal-fear and inflation-fear narratives for long-end selloff may be mispriced; trades premised on term-premium blowout may disappoint.

insights.claim: Gerb attributes the rise in 10-year yields to a higher market-implied Fed terminal rate, shown by the ACM (Adrian-Crump-Moench) 10-year risk-neutral rate rising alongside the Fed dots.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: If yields track expected policy path, Fed communication (not fiscal news) is the key driver of long-end moves.

insights.claim: With US nominal GDP growth around 6.6% and credit growth at 3%, Gerb says a 10-year Treasury near 4% with Fed funds at 3% does not make sense, so markets must price more hawkish policy.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: High nominal growth justifies structurally higher yields; fading the yield rise on 'it's too high' grounds is risky.
insights.quote: nominal GDP is a hell of a drug

insights.claim: Gerb's view since 2025 has been that the Fed/Treasury needed to both expand the balance sheet and hike rates, which played out via RMOs and the Treasury buyback plan while the Fed hiked.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Liquidity injection plus hikes is the policy mix; expect continued balance-sheet support alongside hawkish rhetoric.

insights.claim: Odds of an October Fed hike reached roughly 70% a week before recording but fell sharply after a softer PCE print (with methodology changes), leaving a hold as the base case and the two-year rallying hard.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Front-end pricing is highly sensitive to each data print; volatility in SOFR/2-year trades is elevated.

insights.claim: A coordinated wave of Fed speakers (including Kashkari and Bowman) on recording day steepened the curve by pulling the front end down and lifting SOFR futures, while also helping the long end modestly.
insights.speaker: Quinn (co-host)
insights.so_what: Fed jawboning is now an active market-management tool; curve steepeners respond to Fed-speak days.

insights.claim: The 30-year Treasury yield is at 5.6%, up from 4.6% six months earlier, which the co-host frames as a multi-year technical breakout unlikely to fully reverse even if the Iran war ends.
insights.speaker: Quinn (co-host)
insights.so_what: Cost of money is structurally higher; positioning for a quick return to sub-5% long yields looks unlikely to pay.

insights.claim: Gerb says institutional investors are asking whether to start buying 10-year Treasuries at roughly 5.20-5.30% with 250-300bp of real yield, betting US fiscal looks better than Europe and Japan.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Relative fiscal/supply-shock resilience may attract a bid for USTs versus other sovereigns.

themes.theme: Narrow AI-capex growth and nominal vs real GDP

insights.claim: Gerb says US growth is very narrow: almost all of it is hyperscaler/AI capex, while manufacturing construction from reshoring policies is fading and power and data-center construction are the only rising categories of private non-residential construction.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: US macro is a single-factor bet on AI capex; any slowdown there hits GDP, jobs and earnings simultaneously.

insights.claim: Hyperscaler AI capex (Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft) grew over 90% year-over-year in 2026 but consensus expects growth to slow to roughly 30-35% next year.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: A sharp second-derivative slowdown in AI capex growth is a key 2027 macro and equity risk.

insights.claim: Much hyperscaler capex is price rather than volume: Amazon said memory prices would absorb 30% of its 2026 AI data-center spend versus 8% in 2023-24, and roughly $25 billion of Microsoft's ~$190 billion guide reflects higher chip-shortage pricing.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Nominal capex overstates real GDP contribution; also a tailwind for memory pricing power.

insights.claim: Gerb says recent broadening in US job gains (goods-producing, construction, professional and business services) is almost entirely data-center or AI-capex driven when broken down line by line.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Apparent labor-market breadth is illusory; jobs are levered to the same AI capex cycle.

insights.claim: Gerb flags risks to the AI growth engine: talk of slowing AI model development, electricity shortages, local opposition to data centers, and Chinese models being just as good.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Power, permitting and competition from cheaper Chinese models are the tail risks to AI-dependent growth.

insights.claim: The host notes a meaningful share of corporate profit growth, such as Google EPS, comes from marking AI-lab investments to higher funding-round valuations.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Earnings quality at mega-caps is partly mark-to-market gains that can reverse in a down round.

insights.claim: The host argues that if the long-end rise reflects 6%+ nominal GDP rather than term premium or inflation fears, a 10-year near 6% may not be bad for risk assets, consistent with indices being near all-time highs.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Higher yields driven by growth can coexist with equity strength, unlike fear-driven selloffs.

insights.claim: Gerb thinks US equities, at least a narrow AI segment, can keep doing well as long as nothing breaks, the labor market holds and $5,000 stimulus checks flow, while non-US markets lacking AI capex look more circumspect.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Favors narrow US AI exposure over ex-US equities facing real-world supply constraints.

themes.theme: K-shaped economy: Main Street and housing crushed

insights.claim: Quinn argues everything outside AI and the Mag 7 is effectively in recession, with no jobs, stock gains or capex growth outside AI.
insights.speaker: Quinn (co-host)
insights.so_what: Breadth trades (equal weight, small caps) remain structurally disadvantaged under current policy.
insights.quote: everything is in a recession look at prices of everything except AI in mag 7

insights.claim: Quinn says homebuilders, regional banks, equal-weight indices, small caps and utilities are being decimated by rising yields while tech and the AI trade stay resilient.
insights.speaker: Quinn (co-host)
insights.so_what: Rate-sensitive Main Street sectors are the losers; pair trades long AI/short rate-sensitive have worked.

insights.claim: Quinn contends a hot Main Street economy is structurally impossible alongside the AI boom because the economy is capacity constrained in power and commodities, so broad demand would push rates toward 10%.
insights.speaker: Quinn (co-host)
insights.so_what: Policy implicitly crowds out non-AI sectors; capacity constraints cap broad recovery.

insights.claim: Gerb identifies residential construction employment as a leading recession indicator, preceding past recessions, and notes it has now slowed sharply as housing has been destroyed.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: A leading indicator is flashing; watch residential construction jobs for recession timing.

insights.claim: The co-host estimates a 100bp rise in mortgage costs means financed buyers can afford roughly 11% less house, a severe hit to those without assets.
insights.speaker: Quinn (co-host)
insights.so_what: Housing affordability shock directly pressures homebuilders and housing-linked spending.

insights.claim: Per BLS Consumer Expenditure Survey data, the bottom 30% of US households account for under 15% of consumption while the ninth decile alone is 15.4%, and Gerb says wealthy share is understated because they skip surveys.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: US consumption depends on asset prices via the wealthy; equity drawdowns transmit directly to GDP.

insights.claim: Gerb describes 'trickle down markets': because consumption is ~70% of GDP and the wealthy drive at least 60% of it via stock-market wealth effects, policymakers effectively must keep stocks up.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Implies a strong policy put under equities.
insights.quote: the stock market is the economy

insights.claim: A host questions whether rate hikes even tighten, since the wealthy top consumption deciles hold T-bills and money market funds and simply earn 25bp more.
insights.speaker: host
insights.so_what: Hikes may be partially stimulative via interest income, weakening their inflation-fighting power.

insights.claim: Gerb says the Fed hike mainly restored credibility, after media questioned whether Chair Warsh was a sock puppet for Trump, rather than meaningfully affecting inflation.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Fed credibility, not demand destruction, is what is anchoring the long end.

themes.theme: Fed and Treasury playbook: hike to flatten, engineer captive demand

insights.claim: Gerb thinks the Fed wants lower 30-year mortgage rates to restart housing but cannot cut because cuts would raise bond and MBS volatility and send yields higher, so it talks hawkish to flatten the curve.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Expect hawkish Fed rhetoric aimed at bull-flattening; curve flatteners fit this policy intent.

insights.claim: Gerb likens Fed forward guidance to playing a fish: officials alternate dovish and hawkish talk to keep rate expectations within a range, and will turn hawkish again once diesel-driven inflation hits.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Recent dovish Fed-speak is tactical; don't extrapolate it into a cutting cycle.

insights.claim: The Fed is watching three-month annualized core inflation ex food, energy and shelter, which is trending toward 2%, giving short-term breathing room.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Provides cover for a pause near term despite headline commodity pressures.

insights.claim: Gerb expects policymakers to engineer captive demand for Treasuries: removing SLR constraints for banks, pension plans buying long bonds, and stablecoins buying T-bills at the front end.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Financial repression supports Treasury demand; stablecoin growth is policy-aligned.

insights.claim: Citing LGIM and BlackRock data, Gerb notes US pension plans are on average over 100% funded with ~3% liability growth, so a hurdle rate of about 3.3% can be met with 10-year Treasuries, reducing demand for private equity, private credit and CLOs.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Pension rotation from alternatives into long Treasuries is a headwind for private markets fundraising.

insights.claim: Quinn argues stimulus aimed at supporting equities and liquidity flows directly into commodities: when yields were pushed down, oil rose more than the Nasdaq, worsening the yield problem.
insights.speaker: Quinn (co-host)
insights.so_what: Policy easing is inflationary via commodities; long commodities hedge the debasement path.

insights.claim: Gerb and Quinn conclude policymakers will debase rather than allow a clearing recession, making Bitcoin, real assets and stocks with earnings the destination for real-return seekers.
insights.speaker: Quinn (co-host)
insights.so_what: Supports long-term long Bitcoin/hard assets as a hedge against monetization.

insights.claim: The S&P 500 priced in gold is roughly flat and below 2008 levels, suggesting much of the nominal stock rally reflects dollar debasement, and European indices look even worse in gold terms.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Real equity returns are far weaker than nominal; gold-denominated performance argues for hard-asset exposure.

insights.claim: Quinn notes midterms create strong incentive for market support, though policymakers could instead opt for a clearing event letting demand cool and yields fall.
insights.speaker: Quinn (co-host)
insights.so_what: Political calendar biases policy toward stimulus into midterms.

themes.theme: Supply shocks: diesel, sulfuric acid and Hormuz

insights.claim: Gerb says diesel, gasoline and food prices are surging, with a sulfuric acid shortage, needed for metal refining and fertilizer, crimping industrial activity because the Strait of Hormuz is closed and facilities are bombed out.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Underappreciated input shortages feed through to metals, ag and food inflation.

insights.claim: Quinn argues a potential US diesel export ban would likely reduce diesel output as refiners cut utilization, stoking demand into supply constraints.
insights.speaker: Quinn (co-host)
insights.so_what: Export bans may hurt refiners and global diesel supply; second-order inflationary effect.

insights.claim: Gerb expects Trump will either ban diesel exports or let diesel prices feed into inflation, after which the Fed returns to hawkish commitment to 2%.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Diesel policy is a near-term catalyst for both inflation prints and Fed tone.

themes.theme: Reshoring away from China and imported inflation

insights.claim: US imported inflation is 5.6% year-over-year, with Chinese-origin goods at 3% and Korean semiconductors at 12.6%, which Gerb ties to shifting supply chains away from China.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Supply-chain diversification is inflationary near term; Korean chip pricing power is strong.

insights.claim: Gerb describes a US strategy (Pax Silica) of leading in AI while Japan and South Korea lead in hardware, with Japan committing about $500 billion to US energy infrastructure and data-center capex in exchange.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Beneficiaries include Japanese/Korean hardware makers and US energy infrastructure; policymakers tolerate inflation.

themes.theme: Europe trapped vs Japan winning the export war

insights.claim: Gerb says the ECB is hiking into supply shortages and stagflation under a single price-stability mandate, a forced policy mistake compared with the US.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Divergence favors US over European assets; European growth risk is skewed down.

insights.claim: Gerb argues the real trade war since the GFC has been Europe (Germany) versus Japan for export market share, which Japan has won, with the trade-weighted euro near an all-time high and German exports to China and the US weak.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Strong euro plus lost share is structurally negative for German exporters.

insights.claim: Japan's net international investment position has held steady even as it burns FX reserves to squeeze yen shorts near 160, while the BOJ hikes on strong growth and rising real wages.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: Shorting JPY near 160 risks intervention; Japan's macro is strengthening.

insights.claim: German corporate bankruptcies have exceeded the 2016-2019 monthly average every month since COVID and keep rising, with employment in the largest 10% of bankruptcies also climbing, alongside Volkswagen and BMW job cuts.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: German industrial hollowing-out is accelerating, not stabilizing; negative for German credit and autos.

insights.claim: Gerb expects Europe must eventually choose between currency devaluation to regain competitiveness or continued austerity that hollows out manufacturing, with the AfD's rise under unpopular Chancellor Merz as the warning shot pushing toward re-industrialization.
insights.speaker: Aiden Gerb (guest, head of global macro strategy, PGM Global / National Bank of Canada)
insights.so_what: A policy pivot to weaker euro/re-industrialization would be a major European regime change to watch.

insights.claim: Quinn notes Europe lacks AI, domestic commodities, and national control of money and bond markets, while facing wars on its eastern and southern flanks, leaving it most exposed to external shocks.
insights.speaker: Quinn (co-host)
insights.so_what: Europe is structurally the weakest major bloc under current energy and geopolitical shocks.
